title: The Colour of a Damselfly
section: 讲话 / 报道 / 讲座
transcript: Damselflies can be hard to spot among plants even when the males are brightly coloured. A field class wanted to find out whether the colours they saw depended on where they stood. Students watched the same insects from two points on the bank, one facing the sun and one with the sun behind them. They used a shared chart to record the apparent colour and noted when clouds covered the sun. On clear mornings, some wings that looked bright from one point seemed almost transparent from the other. The difference was less obvious under cloud. The class concluded that a single photograph might give a misleading impression of an insect's colour. They did not measure how the insects see one another, which would require a different approach from observing them with human eyes.

questions.prompt: What question did the field class investigate?
options: Whether a damselfly's apparent colour changed with the viewing position.
Whether brighter damselflies flew longer distances.
Whether cloud cover changed the number of insects near water.
Whether young insects had different markings from adults.
questions.answer: Whether a damselfly's apparent colour changed with the viewing position.
questions.explanation: 野外课想了解观察者站在不同位置时，同一只豆娘看起来是否会变色。

questions.prompt: What remained outside the scope of the exercise?
options: Whether cloud affected what the students saw.
Whether viewing position changed the insects' apparent colour.
Whether a single photograph represented all viewing angles.
How the insects themselves see one another.
questions.answer: How the insects themselves see one another.
questions.explanation: 课堂用人的眼睛进行观察，没有研究这些昆虫如何看见彼此。
